# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 10 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 10 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_010_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 3, Chapter 2

**1** The tower was being built upon a great square rock. This rock was older than the world itself, and the tower was founded upon it. **2** The rock and its gate had been newly cut. Six young men, strong and all alike in appearance, were building the tower. **3** Many thousands of other men were bringing stones for the building — some from the sea and some from dry land. **4** Those from the sea were polished and square; those from dry land were of various kinds — some square, some round, some smooth, some rough. Some of the rough ones fit into the building; others did not fit at all. **5** The six young men were overseeing the whole work. I stood watching the progress of the building. **6** I saw that the tower was rising in a solid and beautiful form. Seven women stood encircling the tower: the first was Faith; the second, Self-restraint; the third, Power; the fourth, Patience; the fifth, Simplicity; the sixth, Innocence; the seventh, Purity. **7** Of all these, the first was the strongest — she was girded and acted with force. The rest, linking hands with one another, danced in a circle around the tower.

---

### Council Notes

The primordial rock (v. 1) is the theological foundation of the tower allegory. Its being "older than the world" aligns it with pre-existent Wisdom (Prov 8:22-31) and with Christ as the rock (1 Cor 10:4). The tower built on this rock echoes Matthew 16:18.

The seven women personifying virtues (v. 6) are the Shepherd's version of the Seven Spirits. They are not merely abstract qualities but living powers that encircle and uphold the Church. Their names — Faith, Self-restraint, Power, Patience, Simplicity, Innocence, Purity — form an early Christian virtue catalog.

The dancing (v. 7) is a striking liturgical detail. In early Christian and Jewish texts, heavenly worship often involves dance (cf. the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice at Qumran; Acts of John 94-96).
